modes.cue_notes: Place a block (or bolster) horizontally across the shoulder blades at the level of the mid-thoracic spine. Lower onto it so the chest opens upward. A second block or rolled blanket can support the head. Arms rest at the sides or spread wide. Legs extend straight or can be in Butterfly legs for additional hip opening. Allow gravity to open the chest and throat over the support.

source: Traditional yin yoga; see Paul Grilley, Bernie Clark, Sarah Powers
notes: Targets thoracic extension and anterior chest opening. Heart and lung meridians run the inner arm and chest wall. A standard counterpose after deep forward folds or inversions.

breathing_cues.entering: Lower onto the prop on a slow exhale, letting the weight of the thorax settle into the support rather than bracing against it.
breathing_cues.holding: With every inhale, allow the chest to dome upward and the collarbones to widen — the breath itself does the work of opening the anterior chest and intercostals. On the exhale, the sternum softens without collapsing and the upper back yields a little deeper into extension.
breathing_cues.exiting: Press the palms into the floor on an inhale to lift the chest slightly off the prop, then exhale as you slide the block away and lower the spine segment by segment to the floor.

modifications.name: Lower block height
modifications.description: Use a block on its lowest setting or a folded blanket instead of a full-height block to reduce the depth of thoracic extension, appropriate for students with kyphosis or thoracic stiffness.

modifications.name: Blanket support under head
modifications.description: Place a folded blanket or second block under the head to prevent cervical hyperextension, especially important for students with neck issues or significant thoracic kyphosis.

modifications.name: Arms by sides
modifications.description: Keep arms alongside the body rather than spread wide or overhead to reduce shoulder demand and maintain a more neutral anterior shoulder.

modifications.name: Butterfly legs
modifications.description: Bring soles of feet together in butterfly legs while over the support to add a simultaneous inner groin opening, deepening the overall effect for students comfortable in the thoracic opening.

emotional_release_potential.notes: The anterior chest and intercostal opening directly accesses lung meridian territory. Grief, sadness, and unprocessed loss are stored here in TCM; long holds over a support may release sighing, tears, or a catching sensation in the throat.
As the chest dome opens over the prop, the protective muscular guarding around the heart and lungs softens. Students may feel an unfamiliar sense of spaciousness that triggers held sadness.
Opening the heart space in a vulnerable supine position is an act of courage. Heart meridian work supports authentic emotional expression and willingness to receive love and connection.
